statement: 2015 changes to the KX250F: a bridged-box piston, a shorter head pipe with the KX450F's larger muffler and a resonance chamber, a heavier flywheel rotor (9.5 kg-cm, with 8.5 and 9.0 optional), a finer 12-hole downstream injector, new valving in the Showa SFF fork, a 270 mm petal front disc in place of the 250 mm, a self-locking rear axle nut with no cotter pin, lighter axles and subframe, a four-position bar mount and two-position footpegs that can be lowered 5 mm.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F motocross test

statement: Testers rated the 2015 KX250F engine the best part of the bike: a very broad, fast powerband, with the upstream injector adding fuel progressively from about 7,000 to 13,000 rpm. It won that magazine's 250 four-stroke comparison three years in a row on the strength of the engine.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F motocross test

statement: The 2015 KX250F changes maps with plug-in couplers: green is standard, white is for soft ground (more ignition advance) and black is for hard, slick ground (less wheelspin). Testers preferred white, and swapping takes under 30 seconds. Launch control is a bar button; testers thought it mainly helps novice starts.

vals.couplers: green standard / white soft / black hard

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F motocross test

statement: Magazine race settings for the 2015 KX250F, for riders over about 170 lb. Showa SFF fork: 0.96 kg/mm spring (0.92 and 1.00 optional), compression 6 clicks out (stock 7), rebound 11 out (stock 10), spring preload adjuster 25 clicks in (stock 8 of 40), forks raised 5 mm in the clamps. Shock: 5.3 kg/mm spring (4.7 to 5.5 optional), race sag 100 mm, high-speed compression 2 turns out, low-speed compression 8 clicks out (stock 11), rebound 13 out (stock 14).

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F motocross test

statement: Testers marked the 2015 KX250F down on handling: slow to turn, the shock wallows and wanders under acceleration in stock trim, and adding front weight to make it turn makes the front tyre hunt. Their fixes were 22 mm offset triple clamps and a longer shock pull rod, which stiffens the first part of the stroke and lowers the rear.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F motocross test

statement: Found on the 2015 KX250F in testing: the stock chain guide wears quickly, the clutch slips under hard use (stiffer clutch springs or an aftermarket clutch were the fix), it shifts poorly under load, and the stock grips are small and hard.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2015 Kawasaki KX250F motocross test

statement: 2019 changes to the CRF450R: revised exhaust ports, larger mid-pipes, a new clutch lifter and pressure plate, two 12 mm scavenge pumps in place of one 16 mm, a five-nozzle piston oil jet, a gear position sensor with separate ignition and fuel maps for each of the five gears, launch control for the first time, no kickstarter boss on the cases, a lighter and less rigid swingarm, a revised shock linkage, new fork valving, bars 15 mm lower on four-way adjustable mounts, lighter footpegs and a front caliper with 30 and 27 mm pistons on a 270 mm disc. Frame geometry is unchanged.

source.name: Motocross Action - race test of the 2019 Honda CRF450

topic: Weight, power and engine character (2019 test)
statement: A 2019 CRF450R weighed 238 lb in testing, about 15 lb more than the lightest 450 that year. It made 60.2 hp on the magazine's dyno, the most in the class. Below about 9,000 rpm it matches the 2018 engine and is linear and predictable; above that it pulls much harder, about 3 hp more at 11,000 rpm, up to the 11,600 rpm limiter.

source.name: Motocross Action - race test of the 2019 Honda CRF450

statement: The 2019 CRF450R has three maps on the bar button. Testers preferred the standard map; the aggressive map feels crisper but made about 1 hp less everywhere on the dyno. Launch control has three rev-limit levels; testers found it worked but was complicated to set.

source.name: Motocross Action - race test of the 2019 Honda CRF450

statement: Magazine race settings for the 2019 CRF450R. Fork compression clicks out: 8 for pros, 12 for intermediates (stock is 12), 13 for vets and novices; rebound 12 to 13 out; fork flush at the stock height. Shock: tested with a 56 N/mm spring (54 N/mm for light riders, with every clicker 4 softer), race sag 108 mm (106 to 110 worked), high-speed compression 3.5 turns out, low-speed compression 10 clicks out, rebound 7 clicks out. The bike is very sensitive to balance: shock changes show up at the fork, and it needs about 108 mm of sag to feel level.

source.name: Motocross Action - race test of the 2019 Honda CRF450

statement: The 2019 CRF450R turns in sharply and is easy to move in the air, but testers found it loose at speed: the front deflects on bumps, it can shake its head on fast straights and the rear steps out under power on corner exit. The fork rides low in its stroke, harsh on small bumps yet soft on big hits; stiffer fork springs or firmer compression valving were the suggested cure.

source.name: Motocross Action - race test of the 2019 Honda CRF450

statement: Found on the 2019 CRF450R in testing: the clutch is the weak point and fades under hard use, the radiators run hot and can boil over (a higher-pressure radiator cap was suggested), the twin exhaust is heavy and the head pipe sits where it can touch the rider's leg, and it measured 117.5 dB on the two-metre sound test.

source.name: Motocross Action - race test of the 2019 Honda CRF450

statement: The YZ125 engine design dates from 2006 and the bike was mechanically unchanged from 2010 through 2012, apart from a 2011 running change: a 75 mm longer silencer with a larger core and more packing, a 430 main jet in place of the 410 and a needle half a clip richer (6BFY43-3 in place of 6BFY42-3). The power valve starts to open at about 9,500 rpm.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Yamaha YZ125 motocross test

statement: Stock jetting on the 2011-2012 YZ125 (38 mm Mikuni TMX) as tested: 430 main jet (a 440 and a 420 come with the bike), 40 pilot, 6BFY43-3 needle with the clip in the 3rd groove from the top, air screw 2 1/4 turns out.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Yamaha YZ125 motocross test

statement: Magazine race settings for the 2012 YZ125, which is mechanically the same as the 2010 and 2011. KYB SSS fork: stock 0.42 kg/mm springs (0.40 for riders under 150 lb), compression 11 clicks out, rebound 6 clicks out, forks raised 5 mm in the clamps. Shock: 4.7 kg/mm spring, race sag 98 mm, high-speed compression 1 1/2 turns out (it is sensitive; adjust in 1/8 turns), low-speed compression 13 clicks out, rebound 10 clicks out.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Yamaha YZ125 motocross test

topic: Weight, power and how it has to be ridden
statement: A 2012 YZ125 weighed 199 lb and made 34.0 hp on the magazine's dyno, within 1 hp of the strongest 125 that year; it is softer from 6,000 to 8,400 rpm and even from 8,500 up. It has to be ridden wide open with the clutch, and rolling off costs momentum. The suspension was rated the best in the 125 class.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Yamaha YZ125 motocross test

statement: For the 2010-2012 YZ125 testers called one tooth more on the rear sprocket the best single change: it makes second gear usable in corners and closes the gap to third. An aftermarket pipe adds about 2 hp. A big-bore kit with a 58 mm piston takes it to 144 cc and needs the centre cases relieved.

source.name: Motocross Action - 2012 Yamaha YZ125 motocross test

statement: On the 2010 YZ125 testers found the steering more relaxed on corner entry than the 450s of the day, good high-speed stability and very good bump absorption, with the bike floating over acceleration chop. It suits riders of about 120 to 190 lb; near 200 lb a rider will want stiffer springs and a larger rear sprocket. It needs constant shifting to stay in the power.

source.name: Dirt Rider - 2010 Yamaha YZ125 riding impression

statement: The 2021 KTM 65 SX is a 64.9 cc liquid-cooled two-stroke single, 45 x 40.8 mm bore and stroke, with a pressure-controlled exhaust valve, kick start, a 6-speed gearbox and a hydraulic wet multi-plate clutch. Weight without fuel is 53 kg. Seat height 750 mm, ground clearance 280 mm, steering head angle 64.5 degrees, fuel tank about 3.5 litres. Brakes are four-piston calipers front and rear on 198 mm and 160 mm wave discs. It is aimed at riders of about 8 to 12 years.

source.name: KTM 65 SX 2021 model information

statement: The 2021 KTM 65 SX has a WP XACT 35 mm upside-down air fork with 215 mm of travel. The air spring is in the left leg and is set to the rider's weight with a hand pump, and the fork is adjustable for damping. The rear is a WP XACT shock mounted directly to the swingarm with no linkage, fully adjustable, with 270 mm of wheel travel.

source.name: KTM 65 SX 2021 model information

statement: The 2017 KTM 350 XC-F is a 349.7 cc DOHC four-stroke single, 88 x 57.5 mm bore and stroke, 14:1 compression, with titanium valves, fuel injection through a 44 mm throttle body, electric start with a lithium battery, a 6-speed semi-close-ratio gearbox and a hydraulic clutch. Stock final gearing is 14/50. Fork: WP AER 48 air fork, 310 mm travel. Shock: WP on a linkage, 300 mm wheel travel. Steering head angle 63.9 degrees, wheelbase about 1,485 mm, ground clearance 370 mm, seat height 960 mm, fuel tank about 8.5 litres (2.25 gal), weight without fuel 100.2 kg. Brakes: 260 mm front and 220 mm rear discs.

source.name: KTM 350 XC-F 2017 model specifications

topic: Rider weight and the stock shock spring
statement: KTM's owner's manual for the 2017 350 XC-F lists shock springs by rider weight only up to 95 kg (209 lb): 39 N/mm for 65-75 kg, 42 N/mm for 75-85 kg and 45 N/mm for 85-95 kg. A rider heavier than that is off KTM's chart. The check is the same as for any rider: set 105 mm of rider sag, then measure static sag against the 35 mm target. If static sag comes out well under 35 mm, the spring is too soft for the rider and a stiffer one is needed; the rate for riders above the chart is not published by KTM. The fork is air sprung, so support at the front is set with pressure from the 9.8 bar (142 psi) standard.

source.name: KTM 350 XC-F 2017 owner's manual, chassis tuning tables
